review_text_raw:
At the time of its release, I was kind of obsessed with Sara is Missing. The style was fresh and new, and what a great idea! Finding a missing person through their phone is already such an interesting mystery, a look at how much of our lives are stored in this technology with a personal touch. However, in the end, I had too many questions that went unanswered, and ultimately felt unsatisfied.

SIMULACRA, on the other hand, has so far fixed all of these issues. For clarity sake, I have only achieved two endings at this time, and have more to go. For the same reason, and to give my respect to the developers, I will say I found this game through NightMind's video. This was one of the very, very few times I actually paused in the middle of a video to go out and buy the game myself - I will admit however, the low price was a factor in that. I was expecting more, but this game was more than worth my money.

There are a few silly little mistakes - Some of which add a level of realism and are undoubtedly intentional, like the varying type styles and occasional grammar errors and misspells... And some which are just a little funny, but in the end, the writing and acting won me over any time I was distracted from the experience. The mystery this time around is far more fun and rewarding to solve, the characters are largely likable (UNLESSANNAWHEREARETHOSEDATAREPORTS) and believable within this context.

The whole theme of using someone's phone to dig through their identity is played with far, FAR more effectively here, and the paranormal aspects (cmon it was obvious) offer some commentary, as well as another interesting character I wanted to explore.

The fact that the game doesn't allow multiple save states to allow choice-scumming for the desired result was at first a bit annoying, I want to see what they would all say if I said this or that, but it does add a certain weight to each choice - If you slip up and don't want to see it through, you have to start over.

There are a few other fun little distractions, if you need a moment of relief from the spooks, such as replying over and over again to the home security bot, replying to other people's tweets with memes, editing Anna's Spark profile the moment you have access to it so that it shows the lyrics to Feel Good Inc. and a picture of her cat, and etc. And even if you do choose to mess around a little it, you can still progress the story whether or not Anna's profile name is now Snart.

While I can't promise poo your pants horror, and the scares will be subjective, it's a fun little game even if you only want to pretend to be another person and gain everyone's trust, or immediately tell everyone you meet that you're not Anna. Or call 911, call her friends, read her texts and emails, waste her phone battery, and etc.

[h1][b] TLDR: While not noteworthy in any direction, it’s a decent low-budget mystery/thriller that is acceptable for its price. [/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Good concept with phone imitation and believable features
➕Multiple decision-based endings


[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Severe lack of options, not even fullscreen toggle or audio options??
➖Missing some essential phone features, like ease of scrolling through tons of text messages or jumping to specific times in videos
➖Some cringe voice acting/FMV

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world takes place entirely on a phone, using the phone's UI screen. It’s a very simple imitation, but most of it works as you’d expect a phone to function. You have various apps that you go through, including email, messaging, Twitter-like  social media, photos, and dating apps. As far as a phone imitation goes, I’d say the world is fairly good, though it is missing some obvious features like being able to click on a point-in-time on a video to move to that section, or scrolling through hundreds of text messages. Otherwise, it’s good. 

The narrative focuses on a girl named Anna, who has seemingly disappeared. For some reason, Anna’s phone ends up in your possession and you have to sleuth around to figure out what happened and how to find her. 
The story has branching paths that ultimately comes down to which person you end up believing and siding with, as well as specific choices along the way that influence the ending of the game. 
I got the “Worst” ending, but was still satisfied with my playthrough because I did everything sensible and logical that I would do. To achieve the better endings, you have to do questionably moral things like [spoiler]siding with a sex offender when you have limited information[/spoiler], or [spoiler]confessing love to Anna’s best friend while pretending to be Anna.[/spoiler] In a way, it's sleazy and morally ambiguous, but I do also understand the phishing aspect of it and needing to obtain information any way possible. 
In the end, I found the story to be only “Ok” . The antagonist of a [spoiler]rogue AI[/spoiler] wasn’t very exciting or scary at the end. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The general gameplay loop is to explore around the phone UI solving puzzles to advance the plot. 
The mechanics remind me of a watered-down version of The Rootrees Are Dead (great game, check out my review [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/Synikx/recommended/2754380?snr=1_5_9__402]here[/url]), how you have to use hints to sleuth around a phone for information. I’d say about 70% of the puzzles in the game consist of either decoding messages or pictures, whereas the other 30% is about researching information. 
The picture/message decoding consists of either aligning pictures correctly, or putting text messages in the correct order. I found the picture puzzles to be much more challenging. The researching of information is where it’s similar to Rootrees where you need to look through emails or messages to find correct information for things like passwords. 
While the mechanics were fine, I would have much preferred the quantity of research to picture/text decoding to be reversed, that is 70% research and 30% decode. I felt like the decoding was a bit out of place. 

The difficulty is generally easy. I was stumped a few times, but the game allows a skip or nudges you in the right direction after a little bit. The only challenging part is figuring out the very specific choices to get the better endings. 

[h1] [b] Technical (Graphics/Performance) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Graphics were okay. Most of the game is a phone UI, with the remaining parts being FMV or pictures. I felt that the UI looks simple, but believable. The FMV and pictures were high quality and numerous, especially in public settings, so I appreciated the realistic approach. I’d say this is around PS4-era graphics. 
Performance was flawless, zero issues. 
I do want to call out the atrocious graphical settings. I don’t think I’ve ever seen a game with less options. I think the only two are language and subtitles. Not even audio volume or full screen or resolution. 
I didn’t notice any bugs. 

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD  

[h1] [b] Audio – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
There wasn’t much, if any music. 
There is ample voice acting, and half of it was super cringe. Anna did a decent job. Greg was just terrible. Taylor has ups and downs. Ashley is decent as well. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
Decent replay value due to the multiple endings, but you probably need a guide for the route on how to get there. Otherwise, just achievements and easter eggs. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Simulacra is a horror game that takes place entirely on a phone screen, with you being the user operating the phone. This isn’t an overly terrifying game, though there is a few jump scares, and I found the plot to be okay, which is generally the linchpin with these more “Visual novel”-type games with less gameplay depth, so all things considered, it’s a fairly good game, especially for the price. 

I don’t have too many big issues with the game, just smaller ones. 
The graphical options are terrible, but thankfully, I was able to use alt+enter to play in windowed mode, since there’s no borderless option. 
I’d have liked better phone functionality, namely being able to click to any point in time for videos and ease of scrolling through dozens of text messages. Everyone has been using smartphones for decades at this point, so these basic features should be available. 
Lastly, the voice acting was pretty cringy. Cringe was generally the norm, with average performances being the exception. 

Otherwise, the gameplay through small puzzles and sleuthing, and the story, while not exceptional, were both enough to keep me interested until I hit the credits. 
There’s a lot of things that could be improved, but for the price, I think it’s a solid game worth checking out. 

[h1] [b] Recommend? (Price) [Y/N] [/b] [/h1]
[h1]Yes[/h1]
$5 is an acceptable price considering it takes around ~4 hours to beat for a single playthrough and offers multiple endings. Sale price of $1 is very good. 

You can find my curator page here: https://steamcommunity.com/groups/Synik_GR

review_text_raw:
[h1]Short but Intuitive Mystery Game[/h1]

[i]SIMULACRA[/i] is a modern FMV game that features great sleuthing gameplay with some minor horror elements. After I 100% the entire game, I can safely say this is one of the better indie visual novel titles I've encountered if not for the gameplay alone. I will try to keep this review mostly spoiler-free, but as usual with my reviews for narrative-based games, I will have spoilers for stuff I feel the need to comment on. 

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[olist]
[*] The gameplay and puzzles are fun yet intuitive. I like the process of fixing corrupted messages and images to not only progress the game but to also discover more about the characters.
[*] Lots of "show don't tell" moments that exemplify how the developers understand that this is a visual medium and that it is important to use the visuals to their advantage. For example, though it's never stated Anna is into fitness, one of the first image puzzles is of her posing with weights to give the idea that she is an active person. This is great  yet subtle storytelling I love to see in these types of games. 
[*] The text messages and dating profiles are pretty genuine. There are definitely people out there who act exactly like the ones in this game.
[*] The narrative does a lot to try and make you question the motives of the characters and their backgrounds in a meaningful way so that the suspense is maintained the entire playthrough. 
[*] [spoiler] The main antagonist being a serial killer HAL-9000-esque AI in the phone itself is fascinating in its own right, and the fact that its goal is to create perfect versions of otherwise "pathetic worms" as it refers to people it deems as as such, is great social commentary on how people are obsessed with their public image online to the point that they are no longer genuinely themselves. The antagonist also serves as a personification of tech companies and their obsession to mold people into their idealized image through deceptive practices and establishing trust by packaging things in digestible ways. For example, during the phone reset, the soothing sounds and use of cool hues is meant to contrast with the otherwise invasive questions and disturbing content the OS system tries to get you to answer in detail. In the end, you get the best ending by impressing the AI with your ability to manipulate the characters--an interesting moral dilemma to say the least!  [/spoiler]
[*] The menus and apps look and feel like their real version counterparts. Very good overall graphical presentation. 
[*] Small and subtle changes to show you are progressing through the story. For example, [spoiler] Anna's picture in the home screen will change expression the closer you get to the ending of the game. [/spoiler]
[*] Lots of small things to discover just by exploring the phone (which you can get achievements for). 
[*] Sped up dialog loading for additional playthroughs is a great QoL feature. 
[/olist]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[olist]
[*] The voice acting and FMV sequences come across as cheesy most of the time, if not overacted. 
[*] The autosave feature means you can't go back to a previous part like you can with most visual novels. This means that if you messed up on a certain decision, you may have to restart the entire run just to redo it. This can be pretty frustrating. 
[*] No option to skip puzzles for additional playthroughs means you'll have to do them over and over again which can be pretty tedious if you're trying to get all the achievements. 
[*] The dialogue choices you  need to appease and have Taylor trust you come across as a bit too flirty at times.
[*] Greg and Ashley come across as too angry and distrustful to the player character depending on certain choices made. Meanwhile, Taylor comes across as too trusting. This is why sometimes it's not very good to have a faceless protagonist--we don't really understand what the characters see in [i]you[/i] when the interactions are so minimal. 
[*] The horror elements are too on the nose with the jumpscares. Though the phone OS does have some good subtle horror elements, more of this throughout the game would have been way better overall. 
[*] [spoiler] Though I like the idea of the antagonist, having it type in predictable shaky font and using distorted visuals is pretty cliche. Personally, I think it'd come across scarier if it were way more subtle like how it is when the phone resets.[/spoiler]
[/olist]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Worth at least one playthrough--though playing it blind is your best bet. The gameplay alone makes it worth it. For additional playthroughs, some patience is required. Watch additional endings via recordings if that's not your thing.

review_text_raw:
Basically "Black Mirror: The Game," which can be a good thing if that's what you're into. It's an interesting premise and I respect them for trying something different, but they fall into the same trap that Black Mirror does: saying "technology is bad!" and hammering that idea home over and over and over for hours gets boring after a while.

Within the first ten minutes, the game does a good job establishing the theme of "Technology connects us but leaves us feeling alone." The problem is that once it does that, it doesn't really know where to go from there. There's no meditation on what we as a society can do to work on this, or explorations of how one can learn to find self-worth in such a shallow world. It's just a repeating loop of talking to online dating matches (all losers and jerks), going through Anna's browsing history (all online shopping and personality quizzes), and texting her ex-bf, who's verbally abusive and cheated on her when they were dating. We get an occasional break when we go through her emails, where we learn that she keeps getting rejected from vet school, her boss is unappreciative, and her co-worker is constantly harassing her.

It's all so...bleak, which is fine, but there's just no point to any of it. Like, okay, I get it, the internet sucks and is making us all act like terrible people, but *what's your point*? Should we do something about it? Or just accept it? 

The gameplay is engaging but not very complex, meaning this game relies on its story, which just didn't have enough depth for me. Maybe it's my own fault for being more optimistic about the state of the world, idk, I was just hoping for a story with something more to say other than "phones bad, am i right?"

review_text_raw:
Great idea, but bad execution. A for effort but C on the result.

PROS:
- Technical polish. The UI looks good and the videos, picture and audio are of good quality.
- The developers did seem to put their heart into this. It is not easy to make games involving so much detail, actors and voice work
- Interesting concept. While not original, piercing the story together through different apps on the phone was neat
- Some puzzles were neat like finding a phone number hidden in Twitter posts or creating a specific Tinder profile, because they fit the concept of the game really well

CONS:
- All the characters are downright unlikable.. I didn't care for Anna one bit and if there was an ending to kill them all off I would have took it. And when I mean all, I really mean all. Every single one, including her mother and the HR lady. I guess only the cat gets a pass and even then I'm not sure
- Unrealistic voice work. Most characters speak very unnaturally. The biggest offender being Greg who talks like he is in a kid's anime
- You can only speak to people when they are online, but they always pop up immediately when you need them to make progress, making it very obvious you are playing a videogame. A few seconds delay would have done wonders for the immersion
- Repetitive gameplay. Most of the time you will be doing the same "construct a phrase" or "remake a picture" puzzle and the whole cycle of restoring the phone data should have only happened once.

A supernatural horror story where you use a missing person's phone (texting contacts/viewing photos/reading e-mail/other apps or social media) to figure out what happened to them. Not the same but it gives a similar feel to me as a game like Orwell.

I don't really enjoy horror games in general so I preferred playing this game as a mystery. I didn't really care for the random 'horror' sound effects or imagery. I was a bit disappointed when the plot went for [spoiler]the sci-fi twist. It's alright but I would have liked a regular, more realistic thing. It felt like something outside of your control with no real foreshadowing or buildup. There is nothing to suggest that it was possible and even after you learn about it you can't go back and see much in a new light. It might be nice if they at least put something random about the dangers of AI or something.[/spoiler]

Aside from the general phone-searching there are some minigames. They aren't too tough but one might be harder if you're not a native english speaker. One minigame is taking a jumbled list of words and making the right sentence out of it. However, it's not enough to get an equivalent meaning- you have to get the word order exactly right. For example, 'Meet me and I'll show ya this weekend' is wrong but 'Meet me this weekend and I'll show ya' is right.

Worth a look if you're fine with learning about the missing person story through phone history and dialogue.

Other thoughts:[list]
[*] It's a little annoying that in order to get the 'good' ending you have to [spoiler]manipulate people because there's no way to convince them otherwise.[/spoiler]
[*] I would have liked multiple save slots.
[*] It's nice that it can be set to automatically skip text on repeat playthroughs.
[*] Pretty much no settings to adjust (only subtitles). I would've liked at least volume and resolution options.
[*] Some inconsistencies/strange things: [spoiler]She met Taylor on Spark but had been following him on Jabbr 3 months ago. Cassie's AMA from 3 months ago is still continuing even though it closed (you get to ask a question)? The article mentions a back-and-forth between genders but you're forced to repeat the female gender and use one of the three pre-selected photos (it seems like other pictures don't progress the story). Why is it assimilating the 'weak'? From what I understand it's somehow taking control of a person and building a world out of their simulacrum (online personification?)? And then discarding the physical body for some reason because they can only lure in one person on Spark before they're useless?[/spoiler]
[*] A bunch of grammar and spelling errors and incorrect subtitles.
[*] Only crashed randomly once.
[/list]

It's been a while since I last played "Simulacra", but since I mentioned it when reviewing "Daemon_9" I felt that it was only fair to give the game it's due. 

As with the aforementioned 'dangerous dark web' title, "Simulacra" places YOU, the player, in the lead role. Not some character. YOU. The premise is a straight-forward one: You have stumbled across some young woman's phone and, in an attempt to discover the owner's identity, you search it's contents, only to discover that the fate of that young woman, may inevitably bring upon your own undoing as well. 

As one can imagine, the very premise of this game hinges on the morally dubious premise that in attempting to find this missing girl, going by the name of Anna, players are consciously violating her privacy by accessing her personal information through her unlocked mobile device. This issue of an individual's right to privacy has been a hot topic for some time now and has been the subject of whole games in of themselves. For "Simulacra", however, this is merely a starting point and one which tells a very different story, albeit one that deals with several other equally relevant issues instead. 

The game feels far more real-world in it's dramatic critique of New Media cultures than that of "Daemon_9", exploring the far more domestic world of mobile device apps and how they can be abused by the wrong kinds of people. Essentially, the digital paper trail that players are encouraged to follow inevitably leads them into the moral grey area of dating apps and 'hook-up' culture, where along with Anna's ex-boyfriend and a somewhat dubious acquaintance of hers, they are drawn further and further into a world that is custom-gear for self-destruction through the distortion of regular human interaction. A common theme in all of these techno-phobic gaming narratives is the belief that they lead to isolation and inevitably the erasure of physical identity by way of hikikomori (feel free to Google search that word if you want to know what it means). "Simulacra" expands this idea to quite a heavy degree, causing players to interact with all manner of "influencers" and shady individuals in order to finally come face-to-face with the kidnapper.   

The trouble with this game in comparison to "Daemon_9" is that while both games involve re-playing old footage and analysing information, "Simulacra" feels like a far more passive gaming experience. Whereas the former game has characters glaring down the barrel of the camera at you, in this instance the game instead tries to maintain at least some degree of a fourth wall. Considering that the whole "Simulacra" experience concerns thrusting the player into the spotlight, this can cheapen the experience with how the player becomes immersed in the experience. Though they are facing the camera front on, actors often look off-camera when performing lines which makes it feel more like a dramatically acted close-up shot to another fictional character than a direct address to the player. Don't get me wrong. The young cast fair very well with the material that they are given and all give admirable performances. It just feels like they were being asked to treat the video sequences more like a piece of scripted drama by the director instead of recreating a piece of Vlog or V-phone footage. When all is said and done, such methods do make the overall experience a little lack-lustre given that one unnecessary degree of separation.  

More promising, however, are the dialogue phases which are conducted through SMS sequences. Here the immersion process is far more convincing, due in no small part to the fact that players are actively engaging with the drama instead of simply receiving video/audio information. The presentation of these sequences also mean that they are not hindered by the usual Stop/Start mechanics to which conversational dialogue phases are usually tied, thus making it feel more natural and organic. This immersion also helps create a sense of helplessness when control is periodically wrested away from the player in a conscious nod to the modern surge of remote hacking and cyber attacks. 

In summary, I do highly recommend "Simulacra" because it is a very good premise for a game. As Major Kusanagi famously said in the conclusion to Mamoru Oshii's "Ghost In The Shell": "The Net is vast and infinite", and as the digital landscape continues to expand the possibilities for new narrative material surrounding new media technologies grows with it. However, as a narrative gaming experience it is a mixed bag. The social commentary aspects of this game, and of it's spin-off "Simulacra: Pipe Dreams", more than warrant at least two full play throughs. However, as far as Interactive FMV dramas go, one is better suited to buying "Her Story", "The Infectious Madness of Dr. Dekker" or the "Daemon_9".

A lost phone appears in your grasp out of nowhere. When you peaked inside, you discovered a creepy video of someone else either asking for assistance or not. In this game, you are abruptly connected to unusual occurrences that put the people nearby in possibly deadly situations.


[H1] Visual: [/H1]
The UX and UI of this game are quite straightforward but interesting in their aesthetic design. Every "app" in this game has been designed in such a way that it is simple to grasp what it is and what kind of hint it is intended to give the player. A genuine smartphone design is featured in the game, along with a number of in-game applications modeled after well-known mobile applications including social media, apps, emails and other type of apps.

[H1] Audio [/H1]
Simulacra's original soundtrack will play during the main menu; it isn't very remarkable, but it wonderfully complements the game. The audio in this game is quite loud and intentionally intended to jump scare the player during the game's horror scenes. The voice acting of the actors aren't really good either. There is nothing else really interesting other than that.


[H1] Gameplay: [/H1]

Simulacra provides a decent horror experience. In this game, the choices you made along the way are tightly linked to one another. This game includes a memo so that you won't get lost if you forgot about the tasks you "need" to do. However, aside from the primary objective—which is to find Anna—they are not really a must-do. It is sometimes necessary to stop doing what you "should" do (based on memo) in order to achieve a different result (that would suit the player better). These messages may appear insignificant, but they contain information that the player will need later on. The difference in outcome will not be visible right away because they are sometimes piling on top of one another before reaching the turning point. The player would also need to uncover puzzles and collectibles throughout the game. In this game, finding those kinds of items is necessary in order to progress the story, unlike other games where they are optional. The puzzles are straightforward to solve; they consist of jumbled words, and all you need to do is choose the appropriate text to complete it. 


[spoiler] If you want to complete the game to the fullest extent possible, you will need to play it more than once because various accomplishments can be unlocked separately and you can only choose one of them. As the game has a few but game-breaking bugs, it would be more practical and less risky to just concentrate on one path at a time rather than reloading a backup save just to get all the achievements in a single run. Although it is possible to do it with the game saves and try to squeeze everything up in one playthrough. I suggest making backup files after chatting with Ashley about "who's at fault."

[/spoiler]


[H1] Controls [/H1]

Keyboard and Mouse are the only way to play it.

[H1] Pricing [/H1]

Worth the price

Simulacra is a game about something. I'm not really sure what, since the game is practically foreshadowing its own inability to deliver on its buildup in many places, and the solution to the mystery had me wondering why there even was a mystery to solve, being that it was something which had little to do with anything that exists in the real world (though there is doubtless some deep philosophical meaning behind the Ghost of Facebook Profiles Past throwing someone off a building for not having enough followers on MySpace).
The story is told through a cast of characters, inlcuding, but not limited to: A man who you can convince to commit corporate espionage and B&E in one sentence each, a sex offender who couldn't shut up to save his life, and the girl who went missing, has her entire character arc revealed in chapter one and never gets any more developement aside from us finding out that everything she did was, in fact, understandable, if rude. All of these reserved seats on the short bus are caught up in a missing person case, but have to do it through the player character, who has his own character, and who can't count to his own IQ. The story is told through tweedle dee and tweedle dum figuring out ways to get more evidence, and the protagonist actually doing it.
The dialogue system is both good and bad. It's bad because the dialogue was bootlegged from Fallout 4, and rarely had the thing I wanted to say, and good in that they actaully manage to do more with it than Bethesda ever did. As stated, the two stooges figure out new ways to attack the case and figure things out, and you actaully do it with puzzling that ranges from "good" to "really bad". There are puzzles where you put together images such that htere's no corruption, which I liked,  puzzles where you unscramble sentences, which were rarely necessary but also rarely obnoxious, and there were puzzles where you have an article to draw information from, but the information in the article is more wrong than the information Bill Cosby the 2nd pulls out of thin air.
Don't worry about the horror elements, it's just a few loud noises and distorted images. So we have a game where the horror is token, the story is confusing, and the characters are dumb and/or pricks. It's technically perfectly adequate, but so are virtually all visual novels, and what extra this does amounts to set decoration. 3/10, since someone who is willing to not think too hard might find it artistically brilliant.

[h1]A First Impression Review[/h1]

I shouldn't have liked this, but I did. I'm not a horror fan, but the concept was interesting enough to keep me hooked. It reminds me of the movie [i]Smile[/i]. It’s creepy and has some jumpscares that make you feel uncomfortable, but the intrigue of the puzzles actually sold me, despite not being a puzzle guy.

[h1]The Good[/h1]
- [b]Realistic Interface:[/b] Feels exactly like operating a normal Android phone. It's natural and easy to navigate.
- [b]Clever Puzzles:[/b] The difficulty is just right. You have to really think, like hunting through emails to find a mother’s maiden name for a password reset. 
- [b]The Drama:[/b] There is a good chunk of backstory in the messages. Reading through the texts, like the drama with the mom, felt realistic and wild. It adds weight to the mystery. It actually made me care about the missing women. 
- [b]Great Price:[/b] This game is cheap. It's under $10 at full price, and catching it on sale for under $2 is a big W.

If you're only just now hearing about Simulacra because it got a sequel, don't feel bad... you're not alone. Somehow this sci-fi horror simulation game ended up flying under the radar of a lot of people until recently. It comes from Kaigan Games, the creators of Sarah Is Missing; a title unavailable on Steam, but is playable for free over on Itch.io. It's a very similar predecessor to Simulacra, and perhaps it helped to serve as an unrefined beta for this more solid-feeling experience.

To say much about the story is to give away the entire game, so to give a very brief synopsis... you found a phone on your doorstep. Opening and accessing its apps leads you to discover that it was previously owned by a girl named Anna. After some digging around in the contents of the device and chatting with her boyfriend and best friend, you realize that Anna has gone missing, and she has been missing for some time. You'll have to recover data, browse photos and videos, and consult with others who were in touch with Anna before her disappearance in order to try and figure out what happened to her, and if you're capable of finding her and saving her life.

The entire game centers around Anna's phone; there's never a time where you will not be using it. The developers have done an outstanding job with creating an entire, believable world within the device; it's fabulously easy to slip into the realm of Simulacra and lose hours of time just checking out all of the dating profiles, work e-mails, and off-beat articles that were added to make the game just that much more realistic. There are several of these websites and news articles to read through, handfuls of in-depth e-mails, tons of selfies of Anna that show off her life and interests, and apps that simulate ones that most of us have installed on our own phones. Of course, a lot of these things are essential components to solving little detective-style puzzles, but there's also a good portion that is just there for entertainment. The game feels like an expansive ARG (alternate reality game), and if one were to play this title on an actual mobile device then the immersion would be surreal.

There are very few areas here that need any work, but the voice acting is one of them. A lot of the voice-overs, especially for Anna's boyfriend, are just embarrassingly cringe-worthy. The acting seen in many of the videos is also pretty bad, but not as bad as the voice work. Those are the only real complaints here, and they're honestly just nitpicky as they can be overlooked with ease. The game's interface is user-friendly, there's a great speed up option unlocked after beating the story once so that players can quickly get to the other four endings (as there are five) and explore different dialogue options, and there's enough small little horror elements to keep the gameplay tense throughout the first playthrough. Overall, it's one of the best casual, story-based sci-fi horror experiences out there right now.

Simulacra is one of those rare gems that manages to slip under the radar of most people; despite being out for almost three years and having over 1,000 reviews on Steam. It's the perfect blend of technology-based sci-fi and subtle horror, in the same vein of TV shows like Black Mirror and Dark Net. While its premise might sound cheesy, this title has some of the most immersive content that I've ever personally witnessed in the thousands of games that I've played. It borders on being an ARG, as there is an incredible level of attention to detail within every app, website, and chat that you'll delve into. Though an initial playthrough only takes about four hours, that time will be sucked away and you'll be left wondering how the hell it got so late, so fast. You'll also be left craving more, so definitely check out Sarah Is Missing and Simulacra 2 afterwards.

After the success of [b]Sara Is Missing[/b], it was obvious [i]Kaigan Games[/i] would continue in the same vein of development. Truth is, before [b]Sara is Missing[/b], there was [b]Finding Home[/b], an indie game also simulating a smartphone experience. Seems the studio entire direction is surrounded by this peculiar genre, one that connects players into a stylized voyeur adventure never seen before.

In [b]SIMULACRA[/b] players gain access to a smartphone belonging to a young woman named Anna. She’s just like any other girl in her early 20’s, working and having a good time with her friends online and offline. All seems perfectly fine, except Anna went missing and she left a strange, bizarre video, as her last registered action.

The overall story is embedded within Anna’s online actions, and each new lead will reveal parts of her past, with phone backups and confessions from her friends. Dialogues are pretty realistic and interesting, making the overall experience more pleasant. There’s no drama, but it’s still somehow intense with a touch of horror and matching jump scares.

Players will explore Anna’s inner secrets and sneak peek into her life, as well as in her problems. Through smartphone apps, such as email, chats, and even the equivalent of Twitter and Tinder, we’ll meet her acquaintances and find clues that may lead to Anna’s whereabouts. While browsing text and pictures, we can restore them by either forming a phrase out of loose words, and building an image by restoring little pieces at a time.

Finding Anna is as much part of the story, as create a connection with other persons of interest through social media. You’ll have to find clues and discover ways to connect with others, to collect new information. [b]SIMULACRA[/b] allows you to open up, or, in some cases, keep pretending to be Anna, which may open up new dialogue options and information.

There’s a certain acquired taste when going through someone else’s life, and the game clearly explores that with decency, but still waving a round or two of peculiar situations and encounters. Some internet references and expressions can be found all over the place, adding a certain style and characterization of realism into that social media life.

It’s one of those experiences, where you’ll forget you’re in the game. As soon as the clues start rolling down and the story involving, it’s a fantastic journey. Gathering clues and finding the direction to go was always relatively easy, and I never found myself stuck or without an idea of where to go. The game also contains a section with the objectives, which will help out in most scenarios if needed.

The visual presentation is accurate and suiting. It’s far more comfortable browsing this virtual phone, then rather use a phone in real life obviously, since the game grants resolutions up to your own. Videos and pictures follow the expected quality and it’s an authentic experience as far as design goes.

Indie games featuring live-action performances with quality are rare. Most of the times the studio goes to an alternative or stylized acting. [b]SIMULACRA[/b] though, doesn’t need any of those tricks, and [url=www.instagram.com/wendyvanhoren/]Wendy Van Horen[/url] plays Anna surprisingly well. Some may claim it’s an amateurish act, but remember, this is Anna’s life, a young person sharing vlogs about her personal life experiences. Wendy definitely brings the character alive, adding a natural and realistic touch.

[b]SIMULACRA[/b] dwells between our presence in the real world, versus our digital personas. I personally think it’s a really good concept and it’s well depict. Doesn’t become far-fetched, even when dealing with the supernatural. It’s a horror experience, but more towards what social media means to us, and how scary it can become. Very entertaining and for the simple price of $3,99 it’s impossible to avoid recommending this one.

review_text_raw:
I enjoy these 'immersive sim' games where you look through devices for clues to a mystery like A Normal Lost Phone or even Hypnospace Outlaw. I liked trawling through old messages and finding tidbits of information that would help me solve a mystery or hack into a passworded account to find more clues. 

I thought that Simulacra would be similar to those kinds of games, but maybe with a more harrowing twist as it's labelled as 'horror'. However I found there to be minimal 'puzzle' elements here, and any that did exist were fairly obvious to figure out. Instead the game is pushed forward by the other characters in the game, who clearly tell you what to do next at each stage.

So the focus of the game is mainly on the story, which I felt was pretty weak. The characters kept railroading me into doing things I didn't want to, like investigating a topic I didn't think had merit, or making me give information to somebody I didn't trust in order to push the plot forward. I thought the final reveal was bizarre and the 'villain's' motives were contrived. It seemed like the devs were trying to send some fancy message about society but hadn't done a good enough job of fleshing it out throughout the game so it all just felt flat at the end.

Several of the other reviews describe the tone of the plot as 'goofy', which I think is fitting but weird for a so-called horror game. Unfortunately the horror aspects solely comes from the occasional jump scare where an image pop ups with a scream, like the prank videos people used to send each other....

And lastly, there are 4 different endings, but getting them is really unsatisfying. To get the best ending, you have to constantly lie to people even if there is seemingly no reason to do so. The middle endings rely on you going out of your way to befriend a random stranger during a potential kidnapping, despite the game giving you many reasons to suspect them. Most people will choose to remain suspicious of every potential suspect but still not lie to anyone, and get the bad ending which makes all your work a waste of time.

review_text_raw:
[b]Last time I pick up a random phone.[/b]

One day, you find a phone just sitting on your doorstep. Like anybody else, you decide to snoop through the phone either to figure out who the owner is so you can return it or just because you can. However, this turns into a much more complicated situation. The first tip off is that while you are blocked by a lock screen, the phone glitches so you can get into it. I don’t know about anybody else, but I wouldn’t have looked through it after that. Anyway, you soon find out that the phone’s owner is Anna and she has recently gone missing. Thus, you decide to look through her phone activity and talk to her friends and acquaintances in an attempt to find her before it’s too late.

There are some puzzles here with the most frequent puzzle you’ll come across involves unscrambling text messages and photos. For texts, you’ll have to order the words in the right order. Photos are more complicated as you’re given several fragments to piece together, but you can’t have any part that is glitched. So you’ll have to figure out which order will allow all glitched out parts to be replaced with the picture. The other puzzle you’ll come across involve you gathering information through either the sites Anna frequented or through her friends. The only problem I had was that some messages had more than one way that it could make sense and that there is an instance where you’re expected to remember certain facts since you can’t go and look for the information.

The acting is average, with Anna’s actress being the stand out, with hilariously bad parts (aka all of Greg’s voice lines) sprinkled in. Voice acting mainly comes through Anna’s vlogs, audio text messages, and phone calls. What doesn’t exactly make sense are the phone calls. At certain points in the story, you’ll get a phone call from one of the characters and you’ll have to answer it (or they’ll keep calling/story won’t continue). Of course, you can’t answer back and when that character asks why you don’t talk back, the excuse is that you can’t make out what they’re saying (despite you being able to hear them fine). I’d rather have the excuse either be that you guess the mic got broken before you found it (which can also imply that whatever is making the phone glitch is causing the mic to stop working) or it auto sends them to voicemail. [spoiler]It doesn’t make sense even more when a police officer actually calls you but assume he’s leaving a voicemail despite not hearing “leave a message after the beep”.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]Also, I just couldn’t help but laugh at the look she gives Taylor in the ending where both of them live.[/spoiler]

Simulacra has four endings each with their own requirements. While you can’t jump to a specific section of the game, you’ll be able to speed things up on your next playthroughs through Begin+. It won’t take long to build up the requirements you need, but the last sequence plays at the same speed.

While Simulacra isn’t perfect, it’s still worth it to experience it yourself, whether it be on PC or on your phone to get the maximum immersion you can. I did find the phone aspect convincing for the most part, didn’t mind that glitches were used to freak you out (though others might not like it), and liked how they filled in the empty space with a room with ambient noises chiming in. There are even some subtle moments here, like the phone’s background changing. The only thing that really messes with immersion is some of the voice acting.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is another game within the sara is missing universe. The first game was good but with new additions to a series brings new mechanics and fixes the short commings of the original, does this game do just that? I will be reviewing the game with a pro/ con style and end with my conclusion.

Pro:
     The game is very creepy. Now jumpscares are cheap and something I dont really enjoy but the game has ambient sound effects that are very spooky. Sometimes you may hear nocking at a door or a wisper or see the lights flicker in your field of view. Some are not really strong in spooking the player but the sound effects really sell the horror.

      The plot is good. Now this is pretty much a horror thriller game that delves with a deep mystery. The game throws you for many loops making you question who can you trust and how much information you should provide. You never know who is at the other end of that text message you recieved. The further you go the deeper the rabbit hole goes.

        The gameplay is simplistic. A game having a simplistic gameplay is nothing to fear. This is like playing a tale tell game where you get dialogue options but sometimes it effects the response of other players and the ending. There are branching paths but not many to get more than 2ish playthroughs. Still it is good to see that some choices creates a response that effect the story and feels a bit like a genuine response in a hypothetical world.

Con:
      There are some puzzles that are difficult. This game has quite a few moments that test memory and makes you search for clues to progress but some of these clues are very well hidden meaning in order to progress you might need to search the internet for the solution to save the frustration. review_text_raw:
Simulacra, developed by Kaigan Games OÜ and published by Kaigan Games OÜ alongside Neon Doctrine, is a gripping and unnerving found-phone horror game that masterfully blends storytelling, mystery, and interactive gameplay. The game places players in the shoes of a person who discovers a lost phone belonging to a woman named Anna, who has mysteriously disappeared. What begins as a seemingly straightforward search quickly evolves into a dark, psychological thriller that unravels through the phone’s contents, offering an immersive narrative experience driven entirely by player interaction with texts, apps, videos, and social media. This innovative format taps into contemporary fears about technology and privacy, creating a tense and intimate atmosphere that keeps players hooked from start to finish.

At its core, Simulacra excels at storytelling through environmental and digital clues, requiring players to carefully sift through Anna’s phone for evidence to understand what happened to her. The game’s interface convincingly mimics a real smartphone, complete with calls, messages, emails, and even a creepy AI assistant named "Maya" that adds an additional layer of eerie presence. Players must navigate conversations, unlock apps, and decrypt files, which gradually reveal Anna’s troubled life and the sinister forces at play. The game’s narrative pacing is well-calibrated, steadily building suspense while offering occasional moments of emotional vulnerability that make Anna’s plight feel deeply personal and urgent.

Visually, Simulacra embraces a minimalistic but effective approach, using the phone’s screen as the main canvas for its storytelling. The user interface is polished and intuitive, making it easy to become engrossed in the investigation without distractions. The game’s use of sound design is particularly noteworthy — ambient noises, notification sounds, and voice messages all contribute to the growing sense of dread. The lack of traditional cinematic cutscenes is replaced by clever interactive sequences that heighten immersion and player agency, ensuring that every discovery feels earned and impactful.

One of the standout features of Simulacra is its branching narrative and multiple endings, which encourage players to explore different paths and decisions throughout the game. This replayability factor enhances the game’s value and allows for varied emotional outcomes, depending on the player’s choices. The writing is generally sharp, weaving together elements of horror, thriller, and drama while avoiding common genre clichés. The characters, though primarily seen through their digital personas, are well fleshed out, and the voice acting adds authenticity to the conversations, heightening the emotional stakes.

That said, Simulacra is not without its limitations. Some players might find the pacing slow during certain investigative segments, and the reliance on reading through extensive text may not appeal to everyone, especially those looking for more action-oriented gameplay. Additionally, the horror elements are more psychological and subtle rather than jump-scare-heavy, which might not satisfy fans expecting traditional scares. Technical issues, such as occasional app glitches or interface bugs, have also been reported but generally do not detract significantly from the overall experience.

Overall, Simulacra stands out as a unique and compelling title that pushes the boundaries of interactive horror by situating its narrative within the intimate space of a smartphone. Its creative storytelling approach, immersive sound design, and chilling atmosphere combine to deliver an experience that feels both modern and unsettling. For players who appreciate mystery, psychological horror, and narrative-driven games that challenge them to piece together a story from fragmented clues, Simulacra offers a memorable journey into the dark side of digital life and human vulnerability.

Rating: 9/10

Simulacra is a Mystery game in which the player is in possession of a missing girl's phone. Using the contacts and apps on her phone you need to track down what happened to her.

Using her phone you will be looking through her life, personal messages and contracts. This will expose you to her life, how she interacted with her friends and colleagues, and what led up to her losing her phone. The transitions of the phone's main image really works well for bringing the horror into the exploration, while the missing information on her phone adds to the mystery between the events.

The puzzles were straight forward, as information I needed to access further parts of the phone easily stood out to me from when I read through her texts and messages. This helped from needing to search through every part of the phone for something I missed.

In all aspects Simulacra feels like a refinement of ‘Sara is Missing’. The texts are not as large and information felt like it was a lot simpler to find, making the game much more enjoyable to get through.

Overall I really enjoyed Simulacra, it may have what feels like weak acting and some moments of absurdity. Yet the character development is great, and looking back on her life and what led up to the moments, with the mystery behind the dating app really made the game intriguing.

[This review made after getting two bad endings out of 5 possible endings]

I like this game and I would recommend it, first and foremost, to players that are interested in STORY or, at least, world 
building. The game is not difficult: picture puzzles, word arranging, and some light fact searching comprise the bulk of the challenges. The meat of the game is in the dialogue choices, and this is where the replayability come from. You don't really get locked out of most options when taking/talking different ways, so you can express your moral flexibility without fearing that you'll reach a dead-end. As for content, they did a decent job of fleshing out with stuff that makes it feel like a "lived with" phone. The game does a good job of simulating smartphone usage with the apps, pics and their poses, vids, and social media content. A nice touch, is that there is a checklist of tasks that would help the truly clueless and serve as a guide for those looking for certain keystone events to play around with on subsequent playthroughs. This checklist is out of the way though for those who don't want hints on what to do next.


On the negative side, some of the voice acting, for me, was off if not "unsuitable". The delivery of the voice only lines truly felt and sounded "rehearsed". The VOs not sounding natural kind of sticks out like a sore thumb amid the aptness of the pictures and videos to a phone setting. The worst offender of this, sorry to say to the voice actor, is the Greg character. Truly, to me, it sounded like he was voicing a cartoon character instead of making a call, and it kind of took me out of the general mood of the game.

I think, the ending, will be pretty hit or miss for some people as well. I want to liken how the ending progresses to one of the scenes in a movie, but that would probably spoil it a bit. It's just that most people that saw it back then went "Wait what was that again?" Don't get me wrong, I'm fine with the endings I got (two bad endings), but the way to the climax was tedious, especially since I don't know if there is a message skip button for when you are doing a replay and you know what is going to be said. A note on the endings I got, it seems like you get locked to a set of outcomes after some threshold. I know my choices at the end didn't end up changing any of my final options. 

All in all, a decent casual horror sim game with some replayability, a fleshed out setting, hit or miss voice acting, and an endgame sequence (not ending, the stuff leading up to the ending) that'll make you go "excuse you? whowherewhenhowwhywhatnow?". 

For now, at full price, it would depend on your affinity for games like these to buy it for around a 5 hour single playthrough (worth it if you go with the $1 per hour of gameplay mindset). It is a decent recommend to buy if it ever has a sale at some point though.

review_text_raw:
A psychological horror/mystery about invading others privacy and cyberstalking?  Talk about checking all my boxes at once!  I'm in!!!

Okay, so this is a little game about you having someone elses cellphone.  I beat it in a few hours, four maybe, and enjoyed the trip.  Everything you have to do in this game, you do with this cell phone.  You get to break into email accounts, search online registries for sex offenders, and catfish people, all in an attempt to find the ultimate truth.  It's like someone finally based a game off my hobbies.

So, the story is kind of linear, in that you work to unlock new areas of the mystery, piece by piece.  First, you get to play with texts and pictures, then you get enough information to open the email, then you can gather what you need to beat security questions...  I'd say the gameplay is about sifting through information to find what you need to move on.  You also get to talk to the phone owner's friends, and they help to move the plot along, or you can ask them for help if you get stuck.

I say it's linear, but there are actually several branching paths that probably all end up in the same place.  Do you know Telltale games?  Kind of like that...  We might make a different turn here and there, but we're all on the same road with a beginning, middle and end.  Example?  Okay, here's an example...  You need to find out some information from this person through text.  Do you own up, tell them you're a creepo reading through someone elses phone because they might be in trouble, or do you try to bluff your way through, pretending to be who you're not?  Make your choice and either way, life will go on.  I don't think you can get stuck.  Then at the end they have a nice little screen that says things like "You and 68% of players looked at the porn stash," just like a Telltale game.  (there was no porn stash...)

It's pretty creative storywise, and I'm not going to give anything away, but it looked like there were about 4 different endings, and I wouldn't be adverse to trying again sometime to see how things can change.  I only had two of them available to me, so I must have needed to do something else to unlock the others, and I'm not entirely sure what that is, which is good to me.  Means the game still has more meat to it.  It reminded me of another game I played called Her Story, and I didn't recommend that one because one play is all it's good for, but this one was more than double the length and I'd be happy to go again some day.

Scariness, it wasn't scary, but I'm pretty tough to phase.  It likes to make creepy noises in your headphones.  There's some image distortion, but I wouldn't call anything a jump scare, which is good, because those turn people off.

TL:DR I had fun.  Maybe you'll have fun too?  I hope I've given you enough information to know if you'll enjoy it too.  That's why I'm writing all this after all.

if you 're looking for an action title, look elsewhere, but if you're looking for an EXPERIENCE that really makes you feel like you're a part of a mystery that needs to be solved, I can't recommend this highly enough. It's fun as hell!

review_text_raw:
Love this game. In the same vein as films like 'Searching', you spend all of your time navigating a device (in this case a phone) in search of a missing person. Simulacra has more a horror tone than 'Searching', but for much of the game's runtime it's only lightly scary, with most of the suspense coming not from supernatural frights but from further unraveling the mystery by feeling like an amateur cybersleuth. 

There are definitely moments where it was frustrating trying to figure out where to go next, but the game generally does a good job of pointing you in the right direction through the use of hints given by the characters in the game. It all feels organic and never too forced. Multiple playthroughs will be needed to see all of the endings, but even just one playthrough will give every player a satisfying experience in the end. 

My few gripes with this game are that the actors aren't really that great in their performances, and for a game that I think is set in the US (at least that seems like the accent everyone is going for), the actor's accents waver quite often. This is obviously not a big budget production, so it's understandable that top shelf talent isn't within reach, but I would say that instead of trying to force a setting, just go with what's available around you. I don't feel that the US setting is necessary to tell this kind of story. I'd also like if there were some way to expedite replays of the game. Yes, if you do a second playthrough you can skip text much more quickly, but I'm thinking of something kinda like Zero Escape: Virtue's Last Reward. In that title there was a branching path menu you could pull up and jump exactly to the point where the story diverged. That would save so much time replaying up until the point where a critical decision was made. 

Conclusion:

Fun cyberdetective game told through a smartphone. Elements of horror, but nothing too overdone so that non-horror fans couldn't enjoy. Gameplay makes you do a fair amount of thinking, without too much handholding, so you feel a sense of accomplishment when you unearth another clue. Tons of easter eggs are there for those willing to look. Performances are not great here, but the voiced parts are minimal and don't interrupt the flow too often.

100% completion

review_text_raw:
Having played "A Normal Lost Phone", the concept of Simulacra isn't anything new to me, however due to this not being a particularly common way of making a game it is a welcome addition to this genre of sorts. 
Simulacra also comes with a couple of different twists compared to what "A Normal Lost Phone" had so it's not complete copy.

The good:
*You are thrown into an interesting story that you have to go through with the help of strangers. Who should you trust? Who should you be weary of? Wel that's the beauty, you don't know and you have to base your judgements on scraps of information that you can find. The story is definitely one of the highlights of this game.
*The gameplay whilst isn't groundbreaking works well for this game and doesn't propose any friction for the player on how to proceed.
*There's a decent bit of replayability in this game if you want to uncover all of the different paths. They also aren't particularly difficult to reach if given enough thought.

The bad:
*The horror elements of this game... Don't get me wrong, I love myself some horror and this game seems like a good candidate for a bit of it, however the way it is implemented in this specific game is forced and cliche.
Build tension through uneasiness, not through awful jumpscares.
*I don't need to be redirected to a webpage with a Discord server every time I finish the game. It is annoying. If I want to join your Discord Ill find a way to do it without it being showed in my face every time.
*For a game with so many branching I feel like it should've had a save system. If you want to get a specific achievement you are forced to replay the whole game. It is remedied by the faster conversations, but I do not want to listen to the same conversation for 7 times just so I can get an achievement.
*The acting leaves some things to be desired. I understand that this is an indie game but the video segments in this game felt somewhat robotic and lifeless.

Overall, Simulacra is a fun and interesting little game, that will not burn a hole in your wallet and will keep you entertained for a day or two. I think its worth giving a try, if you can stand the occasional jumpscare.

review_text_raw:
Although this hasn't dethroned The Black Watchmen for the title of my favorite alternate reality game, SIMULACRA is worth a play for anyone who's looking for something spooky, casual, immersive, and a bit of a brainteaser. The price point can't be beat, though I will say that I suspect that playing the appstore version on your phone would probably be more immersive than playing it over Steam.

The story starts with you finding a phone belonging to an attractive girl named Anna. You're allowed to navigate through her email account, her texts, her pics/vids, and various social media accounts, and you quickly figure out that something is seriously amiss. As you contact her friends, ex-boyfriend and other acquaintances you understand that your role as the player is to do quite a lot of snooping and social engineering to uncover whatever happened to Anna. Your choices are saved throughtout the play and shape the ultimate outcome of the story - I believe there are 4 different endings.

You do need to play it a bit smart; at points you will need to obtain access to accounts and people that are not obvious, which may require you to dig deeper into photos and media feeds to discover the information you need. I did not find any of the 'puzzles' overly difficult, but a few did give me some pause while I dug up the information needed to continue.

There is both live acting and voice acting throughout the game, so you definitely need your sound on to play. Some of the voice acting seems very forced (and some voice actors in particular are rather annoying to listen to) but the pics and vids felt real enough and the chats you have with other characters did a good job of giving each one a solid personality.

There is a horror element to the story, but I did not see any overt gore or violence from my own playthrough. There is something of a jumpscare towards the end, but nothing too bad. Lots of Exorcist style demon-grumbling, static, spooky messages and so on to set the mood as you go.

So overall, for the price, it's a worthwhile buy if this type of game appeals to you.

review_text_raw:
[h1]Final Verdict: Buy! Spoiler-Free Review.[/h1]

This game took me about 3.5 hours to complete on my first playthrough (there are alternate endings available). I tried to read every bit of text and watch every video / photo involved. This game does disappoint as a horror game, but as a mystery thriller, it is excellent. 

This is not a mixed or alternate reality game where you search the web for answers or give your e-mail. The experience is pretty linear, although you can make different choices, the experience goes pretty much through the same set of main events (except for the endings which can vary). You will be looking through videos, photos, Jabbr (facebook), Spark (Tinder), the web (in-game only browser), phone numbers, and e-mails. You simply have to find the relevant information to unlock passcodes or find connections to progress the story. 

You will also have dialogue choices. Some of those choices can have an impact on the story, for example, having more trust with that person and thus giving you a different ending. The story starts out very strong when it is a mystery about what happened to the missing woman, Anna. Even the creepy stuff is exciting at first when you see the distorted videos and the atmosphere leaves things to the imagination. The dialogue between characters is well-written. 

Unfortunately, when you find out the mystery then the horror elements become more silly than scary. I actually just started to troll everybody, trying to get the worst possible ending. There was some real tension at the start and middle of this game, but towards the end, I really didn't feel any connection to any of the characters or "the danger" involved.

That's a shame because this is a very polished experience. The actors all did a nice job overall (sure some of the acting could have been better, but it's better than what is in most games). The mystery sequences where you're sleuthing and trying to find the truth all work extremely well. It's just too bad it ends in a whimper instead of a bang.

[b]Rate 7/10. I still recommend this. With a better ending(s), this could have been something very special. Good overall, but should have been great![/b]

Now this is how you do a smartphone mystery right. The concept of Sara is Missing was sound, but the execution was poor. However, Kaigan Games took the concept and criticism, and further developed the core concept further in Simulacra. 

Simulacra does a fantastic job in making you the player feel lost and isolated. You are in a dimly lit room with constant noises around you - you are never allowed to feel comfortable where you are, or with what you are doing. You have a random woman's phone, and it is up to you to find her. You have to dig through her e-mails, Jabber and Spark accounts, and decide which of her friends and acquaintances can be trusted with crucial information related to Anna's disappearance.

The tension is real. Should you really be doing this? Wouldn't it be easier to just contact the police? But can the police even find her with so little information? Which of her friends can be trusted? Could one of them be responsible for her disappearance?  The whole time something feels off from the very beginning. Are you being watched? 

The only real gripe I have with the game is the jump scares. Jump scares are for cheap low-level horror titles. And I don't necessarily mean cheap in terms of dollar value - a lot of AAA titles misuse jump scares and it's pathetic. One or two carefully placed jump scares in appropriate games is fine, but Simulacra isn't one of them. The fear comes from the tension and subtle little nuances. When the phone goes crazy and suddenly the picture of Anna on the wallpaper changes slightly, but you're not sure if you imagined it or not - perfect. Loud noises and jumbled up pictures - stupid. 

All-in-all Simulacra is a terrific experience if you like these kind of horror games. Don't let Sara is Missing deter you from trying out Kaigan Games other titles, unlike a lot of other developers, they took the criticisms they received and learned from them to craft better experiences. That alone makes this game worth checking out.

8/10

A very interesting and well done horror game about fiddling with a stranger's phone.

Before Simulacra, the devs made Sara is Missing, a game following the same line (horror game about exploring someone's phone) and, in Simulacra, it's easy to notice how much the game has evolved. While in SIM there were some choices to be made but ultimately they didn't change all that much, in the case of Simulacra it actually changes, with 4 possible different endings depending on what you do during the game.

The game involves talking to people using the phone's messenger app, browsing through other apps, searching for clues and solving some puzzles, while experiencing some creepy things on the way. The story, although somewhat linear (with some differences based on your choices) is interesting and well done. Beating the game once also allows the player to start a new game with faster text speed, which allows for faster playing in order to obtain the different endings.

I think the only two things I feel the game could have done better is that, first, it could have been a little more creepy. Not that it's not creepy - it certainly is - but it's also a little predictable. It could have had some less predictable moments like [spoiler]weird messages showing up in the middle of normal conversations, creepy pictures/videos opening out of nowhere, etc[/spoiler]. The second thing being that there are a few conversations (not many however - just a few) that go on for longer than they need to, sidetracking into subjects that aren't ultimately important when you're trying to find a missing person.

Nonetheless, a very good game and easily worth its asking price.

Also, for anyone who likes this game, I'd also suggest the free game they have released also from the Simulacra series, called "Simulacra: Pipe Dreams".

A short supernatural investigative game that involves interacting with a cell phone which was left for you to find. You are given the task of finding out what happened to a girl named Anna whose phone you are now in possesion of. You investigate by interacting with individuals in her social media, dating app, email, phone contacts, and other media. Mostly you will choose from a pre-defined list of responses and actions, but there is some free play at times. 

There is a small puzzle element in that you need to "decrypt" her scrambled photos and text messages but it's fairly minor and doesn't really add anything to the experience. 

I have no idea if this was a mobile game first, but it does seem pretty ideal to be a mobile title. It still plays well on PC, but you'll be staring at the image of a phone 95% of the time. I use a dual monitor setup with my left monitor in portrait and my right in landscape so this was ideal to play on the portrait monitor while multitasking. 

I generally do not enjoy point and click, visual novel, or horror themed games and I would probably not place this game in any of those categories. There are some small horror elements which amount to a couple creepy photos and some creepy sound effects, but they're minimal. 

I received this as part of the humble bundle monthly subscription. I otherwise probably would have never purchased this game due to the misleading tags in Steam, but if I had paid the full price at the time of this review, I would have have regretted the purchase. I'll likely buy and play the sequel shortly. 

I found this very similar to Orwell, so would recommend it for fans of that title.

Unsettling. Unseen horrors. You feel as though you truly found someone's phone and have to uncover all their dark secrets to find out what happened. 

Simulacra is an amazing little rabbit hole of a game; a found‑phone thriller that feels intimate, invasive, and surprisingly reactive. Even though my first playthrough ended in the bad ending, with both Taylor and Anna dying, it didn’t sour the experience at all. If anything, it made me realize just how many branching paths and character‑shaping choices I’d only brushed past.

What stands out most is how much influence you actually have over the people you’re texting. The tone you take, the pressure you apply, the empathy you show (or don’t); it all ripples outward in ways that feel organic rather than scripted. That makes every conversation feel like a little puzzle of its own, and it’s easy to get pulled into the illusion that you’re really trying to save someone on the other end of the screen.

There’s also a surprising amount of content tucked into the phone that I completely missed on my first run. I was so worried about the battery dying that I missed returning to the emails and missed the final vlog. That tension is part of the charm, though;  the sense that you’re racing against something truly evil on the other side of the screen.

The result is a game with genuine replayability. Multiple endings, branching character arcs, and hidden threads make it worth diving back in, especially once you know the stakes and can explore the phone more confidently.
If you like narrative mysteries with a voyeuristic twist and choices that actually matter, Simulacra is absolutely worth your time;  even if your first ending is a tragic one.

I watched a playthrough of this game back in 2018, and I remember really liking it back then! When I was reminded of it's existence and heard positive buzz around it, I decided to try my hand at it. It is rather dated in some ways - the inclusion of a Twitter parody app, for one, and even the way characters post on that app scream early 2010's, and the other ways it's aged are just simply Millenialcore humor throughout - it also has quite a few typos (some more distracting than others), some of the voice acting is rough ("fuuuuuck thiiis sooooo muuuuuch" is now a repeated reference in my friend group for the absolutely baffling delivery lol). The plot and gimmicks are also rather predictable if you're at all familiar with this sub genre of horror media and akin sub genres. I recall the plot beats and phone gimmick/framing device being somewhat novel back in 2018, but maybe I misremember.

All that being said, I do enjoy this game and I think it's still worth playing! Some of my favorite things about this game are the soundscape (particularly the knocking and breathing noises randomly interspersed throughout), the interactivity and surprisingly accurate app design/aesthetics for some of the apps also helped immerse me, and I found myself very endeared to Anna and Ashley. This game is no masterpiece, but it's alright for what it is. I'd recommend you play it with a couple friends on voice call - y'all will have a good time leaving nonsense comments on the Jabbr posts, bullying Greg, being irked by Taylor, and making a bizarre dating profile!

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is a visual novel with some minor horror elements told through a phone.

The basic story is woman goes missing and you end up with her phone. You go through it opening apps, texts, emails, etc, attempting to track her down.

The gameplay is divided into 2 main sections. The first is texting back and forth with people in her text/dating apps. The 2nd section is puzzle based where you need to find/figure out some piece of information to proceed. The game gives you little hints in what you should currently be looking for.

On the plus side: There's some branching paths in response choices that can lead to amusing things happening with various characters. It has multiple endings. Puzzles are actually fairly decent. There're some easter eggs/other things you can mess around with and be amused by.

Looking at the downsides of this: Once you have the whole picture of what's going on, the plot and parts of the story don't make much sense in how they would've play out. The characters aren't that good and one of them is written to be unlikable. Occasionally you'll get video messages and the acting certainly isn't good. Occasional misspellings or responses that don't make much sense. The horror element is more of a background thing, so don't expect it to stand out and be prevalent throughout.

Overall, it's a decent visual novel with some options to fool around with. It's not exceptional in any way, but it's different than standard VRs and has some actual gameplay elements to it, which is nice.

I'm a huge fan of this kind of voyeuristic mystery genre, and this is one of the best I've come across. 
The mixing of platforms; text, audio and FMV, creates a very realistic and immersive phone to explore. The level of detail inside the phone apps is also unparallelled. You can explore people's profiles on the dating app and strike up a conversation with someone inconsequential, you can read comments on posts on the social media app, you can read spam emails. So much detail was put into building the world.
The characters (while the voice and visual acting can be a little hokey) each have their own distinct personalities through texts and messages, the writing there is spot on, plus you can interact with them in so many different ways it feels like your voice really matters to the plot.   
I was put off this game initially because I'm a huge wimp and not a big horror fan, but the scares never made me want to stop playing, and it was really worth it.
11/10 I can't wait for the next game from these guys.

review_text_raw:
An extremely interesting experience that goes a bit south near the end. 

Simulacra takes place entirely on the phone of Anna, a missing young woman. The player is in posession of her phone, trying to solve the mystery of her disappearance by talking to her friends and enemies, and logging into her various social media accounts. You never know who you can trust, and there's a menacing supernatural element in the background that builds suspense. 

This is all extremely compelling, and it was hard to stop playing- however once the truth is revealed and you come face to face with what's responsible, it takes you right out of the game. It's not enough to tarnish the whole experience, but I really wish they had gone in a different direction.

You can replay the game for alternate ending sequences and achievements but the overall story will not change drastically, still it might add in some additional hours of play for completionists.

Despite what I consider a disappointing conclusion, I strongly recommend playing through this.
